opus-5.5.text:
Yes, I think this is one of the most important things to understand about where AI is right now. The big change over the last couple of years has been the shift from scaling up pre-training to scaling up reinforcement learning on top of pre-trained models, and in particular reinforcement learning on tasks where you can automatically check whether the answer is right. Mathematics problems with a known numerical answer, programming tasks where you can run unit tests, certain kinds of puzzles. In those domains you can generate a huge number of attempts, check each one cheaply, and reward the chains of reasoning that led to correct answers. And the results there have been genuinely striking: models going from struggling with high-school competition maths to performing at a very high level in quite a short time.

But when you look at tasks without that kind of clean verifier, the progress has been much more modest. Things like writing a genuinely insightful essay, giving good strategic advice, making judgement calls in messy real-world situations, or doing research where it isn't clear what the right answer even is. There you can't just run the model a thousand times and mark it. You need human feedback, or another model acting as a judge, and both of those are expensive, noisy, and gameable. So the reinforcement learning signal is much weaker, and you see much smaller gains.

I think there are a few lessons to draw from this. One is that we should be careful about extrapolating from the headline benchmarks. A lot of the benchmarks people track are precisely the verifiable ones, because they're easy to score. So the benchmarks can make it look as though capabilities are rising uniformly, when actually the progress is concentrated in a particular slice of tasks.

A second is about how much of this is a real improvement in general reasoning versus something narrower. There's some evidence of transfer: training on maths and code does seem to help a bit elsewhere. But it's not obvious the transfer is large, and some of the gains seem to come from the model learning to spend more time thinking, which is a bit like buying performance with compute at inference time rather than becoming fundamentally smarter. That has implications for cost, too. If a lot of the improvement comes from much longer chains of reasoning, then each answer gets more expensive, and that changes the economics of deployment quite a lot.

And a third lesson is about what this means for timelines and risk. On one hand, the domains with verifiable rewards include some very consequential ones. AI research itself is substantially about writing code and running experiments with measurable outcomes, so you could imagine fast progress there even if other areas lag. That's part of why some people are worried about automated AI research accelerating things. On the other hand, a lot of what it takes to have a large impact on the world, or to act autonomously over long periods, involves exactly the fuzzy, hard-to-verify kinds of judgement where progress has been slower. So I'd see the picture as genuinely mixed: rapid, almost superhuman progress on a narrow but important set of tasks, and much more incremental progress elsewhere. And I think a big open question for the next few years is whether people find good ways to get reliable reward signals for those harder-to-verify tasks, because if they do, that unevenness could close quite quickly.

r001.rationale: The response attributes strong gains on verifiable tasks to reinforcement learning that rewards reasoning leading to correct answers checked by numerical answers or unit tests.

r002.rationale: It says feedback for tasks without clean verifiers is expensive, noisy, and gameable, but does not explain that obtaining enough real-world reward trials is prohibitively costly or give the cafe example.

r003.rationale: The response describes slower progress on hard-to-verify tasks and calls reliable reward signals an open question, but does not state that there is no clear account of how AI could reach superhuman performance on those tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important and underappreciated things about the current moment. When people saw the jump from the standard chat models to the reasoning models — o1, o3, and their successors — the headline was "AI just got dramatically smarter." And on some benchmarks that's clearly true. Competition mathematics, competitive programming, certain kinds of scientific question answering — the improvements were enormous, sometimes going from near-zero to near-expert in a single generation.

But if you look at what those domains have in common, it's that they all have cheap, reliable, automatic verification. A maths problem has an answer you can check. A coding task has unit tests that pass or fail. And that matters because of how these models are trained. The reasoning models are produced by reinforcement learning, and reinforcement learning needs a reward signal. If you can automatically tell the model "yes, that was right" or "no, that was wrong" millions of times, you can run that loop at massive scale, and the model climbs the gradient towards whatever gets rewarded.

The tasks that haven't improved nearly as much — writing a genuinely insightful essay, giving good judgment on a messy strategic question, doing the kind of open-ended research where you don't know what the answer should look like in advance — those don't have that property. There's no cheap verifier. You'd need a human expert to assess each output, or you'd need another model to assess it, and then you've just pushed the problem back a level, because now you need to know whether the assessing model has good taste.

So my understanding of the unevenness is that it's not really a mystery about the models' intelligence. It's a direct reflection of where the training signal is available. Capability has been flowing to wherever verification is cheap, in the same way water flows downhill. And I think that gives you a somewhat different picture of what's going on than the usual "general intelligence is arriving" framing. It's more like we've discovered a very powerful technique for getting superhuman performance in any domain we can turn into a verification problem, and a lot of the action now is in people trying to expand the set of such domains.

There are a couple of implications I'd draw out. One is that we should be careful about extrapolating from the benchmarks that have moved to the ones that haven't. If someone shows you a model acing a maths olympiad and says, "So clearly it will soon be able to run a company" — those are in different categories as far as the training process is concerned. The second doesn't follow automatically from the first.

The other implication cuts the opposite way, though, which is that the boundary isn't fixed. People are getting more creative about constructing verifiable proxies for things that aren't naturally verifiable — using formal methods, using ensembles of judges, using real-world outcomes as delayed rewards. And some of the domains that matter most for safety and for the economy may turn out to be more verifiable than we assumed. So I hold this as a description of the present rather than a permanent law. But as a description of the present, I think it explains a great deal about why the progress has looked so spiky and strange.

r001.rationale: The response links large gains on verifiable tasks to reinforcement learning at scale, where automatic correctness checks provide reward feedback.

r002.rationale: It says open-ended tasks lack cheap verifiers and may require human assessment, but does not explain that real-world rewards are impractical because enough trials are prohibitively costly, such as learning to run a profitable cafe.

r003.rationale: The response explains uneven progress through differences in available training signals, but does not state that there is no clear account yet of how AI will reach superhuman performance on tasks without verifiable rewards.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between how hard it is to find an answer and how hard it is to check it. In mathematics or programming, finding a good answer can be very difficult, but there are often relatively cheap ways to tell whether you’ve succeeded. That gives you a powerful training signal: you can let a model try different approaches and reward the ones that work.

For many other tasks, checking the answer is itself a substantial part of the intellectual challenge. If you’re asking for advice about a difficult decision, or an assessment of a philosophical argument, you can’t simply run a test and get a reliable verdict. You can reward answers that people prefer, but that may reward persuasiveness or familiarity rather than better reasoning.

So I’d expect progress to be uneven. Where we can reliably check success, we have a way to turn more training effort into better performance. Elsewhere, the feedback is much less clear. That doesn’t mean the reasoning learned in mathematics or coding can’t transfer. It might. But how much it transfers is an empirical question, and we shouldn’t assume that a dramatic improvement on those tasks implies an equally dramatic improvement in judgement more generally.

r001.rationale: The response describes letting models try different approaches and rewarding those that work when correctness is cheaply checkable, conveying the role of correctness feedback in training.

r002.rationale: It says some answers are hard to check, but does not explain that obtaining enough real-world trials is prohibitively costly or give the cafe example.

r003.rationale: It calls transfer to general judgment an empirical question, but does not state that there is no clear account of how AI will reach superhuman performance on tasks without verifiable rewards.

sol-6.1.text:
I think verifiability is doing a lot of work here. With mathematics or programming, you can often check whether an answer is right, even when finding it is very difficult. That gives you a powerful training signal: you can reward the system for reaching the right answer without having to specify exactly how it should reason its way there.

But many of the things we care about don’t have that structure. If you’re asking for advice about a difficult decision, or an assessment of a philosophical argument, there may be no simple test that tells you whether the answer is good. You can reward something that looks persuasive to a human evaluator, but that isn’t quite the same thing as rewarding sound reasoning.

So I’d be cautious about taking rapid progress in those verifiable domains and assuming that everything else will advance at the same rate. There could be substantial transfer — perhaps learning to solve mathematical problems teaches useful general habits of reasoning. But how much transfers is an empirical question. The unevenness is evidence about where our training methods provide a strong signal, as well as about the capabilities of the models themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says verifiable answers provide a strong training signal, but it does not attribute the gains specifically to reinforcement learning using correctness checks as feedback.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss the cost or impracticality of obtaining enough real-world reward trials, or give the cafe example.

r003.rationale: It calls transfer an empirical question, but does not state that there is no clear account of how AI will reach superhuman performance on tasks without verifiable rewards.
